comments.author: @roberthoople
comments.text:
Honestly, the cost could go quite a bit over that "break even" point, as long as we take features and long-term benefits into account.

For one, Google's Net in the Sky would enable direct mobile connections to consumers, which could have far lower latencies and faster response than current AI over network is.

For two, the Space economy is coming, one way or another, and this is a really good reason to get some more infrastructure out there. In other words, it can help Cement Google's place in the future.

For three, the more things we start doing in space (and I think we should be doing way way more in space, like carbon nanotube manufacturing and particle colliders), the more economies of scale begins to kick in, and a big project from Google is exactly the kind of big space project that can create a lot of downstream innovations, efficiencies and cost-savings.

And I say all that, as my mind screams at me at what an utterly terrible idea it is, to start creating a literal Net of powerful Artificial Intelligence in our Sky. But, they're gonna do it anyways, so I guess I can at least hope for some long term space benefits, before our total doom.

comments.text:
1/ The ISS with all of its panels and size, generates about ~ 200kw.  An Nvidia NVL72 consumes about 120kW.  We would x2 energy capture by always pointing at the sun. And solar panels could get about twice as good.  The surface area of the solar in the ISS is about 2500m2 -> that means an NVL72 needs about something that is 20m2... about the size of your house, to power something the size of a cupboard.

2/ That heat generated by the compute, needs to be radiated back into space.  The ISS needs 160m2. A similar calc for the NVL72 could use the back-side of the panels.

3/ Compute still needs batteries because the energy demand isn't constant because compute requirements aren't constant.

These are the basics (vs all of the other things in that paper)... it adds of that adds weight, which has to be hoisted into orbit.

Lets not forget that the data has to get-up-there and come-back to where it is being used (space-compute to mine Bitcoin seems like a bit of a waste), so those solar panels shouldn't interfere.  And still need ground stations.

There will be a call for a some local-compute, but on-planet will win because it is cheaper and easier.

It's cool - and maybe even technically achievable - but I can't see how this could be remotely worth it from an economical perspective.
The great solar energy efficiency isn't free when you have to send the hardware to space. That's a massive up-front cost. You would need a staggering amount of them to equal a fraction of a current terrestrial datacenter. And how do you deal with the heat generated? if we are talking about significant power - there will also be a troubling amount of heat - and that can be very difficult to deal with in space, especially when your orbit is in constant sunlight. It's possible - but you now need to dedicate a lot of mass for inefficient radiative cooling systems.
Maintenance, upgrades or fixing physical issues becomes impossible to boot.
I just can't see how the math could work out compared to just building green energy terrestrially.
